extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and structural standards for composing and distributing press releases (media releases), including recommended elements, length, distribution models, embargo practice, and multimedia variants. Targets professionals preparing releases for news media or self-distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Letterhead or Logo
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include the issuing organization's letterhead or logo at the top of the release to identify the source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media Contact Information
rubrics_metrics.description: Media Contact Information – name, phone number, email address, mailing address, or other contact information for the public relation (PR) or other media relations contact person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide clear contact details so journalists can follow up. Include multiple contact methods where possible (phone, email, mailing address).

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline
rubrics_metrics.description: Headline – used to grab the attention of journalists and briefly summarize the news in one to six words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep headlines short (1–6 words) and focused on attracting journalist attention while summarizing the news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dek (Sub-headline)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dek – a sub-headline that describes the headline in more detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a dek to provide extra context or detail that the headline cannot convey in its limited length.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dateline
rubrics_metrics.description: Dateline – contains the release date and usually the originating city of the press release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include accurate release date and originating city. If the date listed is after the date the information was actually sent, the sender is requesting a news embargo.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduction (Lead) with Five Ws
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduction – first paragraph in a press release, that generally gives basic answers to the questions of who, what, when, where and why.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The lead should concisely answer the five Ws so a journalist can immediately understand the core facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Body (Supporting Detail)
rubrics_metrics.description: Body – further explanation, statistics, background, or other details relevant to the news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the body to expand on the introduction with evidence, quotes, statistics, background, and contextual information journalists can use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boilerplate (About Section)
rubrics_metrics.description: Boilerplate – generally a short "about" section, providing independent background on the issuing company, organization, or individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include a concise organizational summary (boilerplate) that explains who the issuer is and provides consistent background copy for all releases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Close Conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Close – in North America, traditionally the symbol "-30-" appears after the boilerplate or body and before the media contact information, indicating to media that the release has ended. A more modern equivalent has been the "###" symbol. In other countries, other means of indicating the end of the release may be used, such as the text "ends".
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terminate the release with an appropriate end marker (e.g., -30-, ###, or 'ends') so journalists know the content has concluded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Length and Paragraph Structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations professionals often follow a standard professional format for press releases. Additional communication methods that journalists employ include pitch letters and media advisories. Generally, a press release body consists of four to five paragraphs with a word limit ranging from 400 to 500. However, press release length varies and can range from 300 to 800 words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for 4–5 paragraphs and ~400–500 words as a guideline, but adjust between ~300–800 words depending on news importance and medium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline Purpose and Style Constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Press releases are typically delivered to news media electronically, ready to use, and sometimes subject to 'do not use before' time, known as a news embargo. Using press releases can benefit media corporations because they can contribute to reducing costs and improve the amount of material a media firm can output in a certain amount of time. Although using a press release can save a news outlet time and money, it constrains the format and style of its content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write copy that is 'ready to use' for journalists but be aware that pre-packaged style constrains editorial voice; avoid jargon and craft copy that can be easily adapted into news stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution Models
rubrics_metrics.description: Distribution models: traditional distribution hires a publicity agency to write and distribute to newswires; an alternative is the self-distributed press release, sent directly to media or via free and paid distribution services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose between using a newswire/publicity agency for broad scattering or self-distribution (direct or via services offering localized contact lists). Consider audience, budget, and need for localized lists or monitoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-Distribution Best Practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-distributed press release: press releases are either sent directly to the media or sent via free and paid distribution services. Distribution services often provide localised, pre-made media contact lists which can be used during distribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When self-distributing, use reputable services for contact lists and targeting; expect the content to be provided to outlets 'as-is' and plan for follow-up outreach to priority journalists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embargo Handling
rubrics_metrics.description: If a (draft or final) press release is distributed in an authorized way before the information is intended to be released to the public it is typically subject to an embargo against publication. An embargo requests that news organizations not report the story until a specified date or time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remember: unless a journalist has signed an NDA, they have no legal obligation to honor an embargo; embargo violations risk damaging relationships and may lead to blacklisting. Only share embargoed information with journalists you trust or who commit to withholding publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Video News Releases (VNRs) Guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Some public relations firms send out video news releases (VNRs) which are pre-taped video programs or clips that can be aired intact by TV stations. Some broadcast news outlets have discouraged the use of video news releases because of citing a poor public perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If producing VNRs, be aware of production costs and the potential for negative perception; consider tailoring VNRs for web/podcast formats and community websites to extend reach, but expect some outlets to avoid them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press Releases as Primary Sources and Framing Risk
rubrics_metrics.description: A press release is considered a primary source, meaning they are original informants for information. Press releases can be favorable towards the organization that commissioned or issued them, framing the topic according to its preferred criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize press releases may present biased framing. For credibility, include verifiable facts and be prepared that journalists will (or should) fact-check and contextualize the claims.
